newsitem.title: PERU: 1996 was Peru's Year of the Disaster.
newsitem.headline: 1996 was Peru's Year of the Disaster.

text.p: If Peruvians have one wish for 1997, it is that the events of 1996 will not be repeated.

As they started the New Year with the nightmare of 81 hostages still living under the gun of Marxist rebels, memories returned of last year's grim litany of plane crashes, earthquakes and horrific accidents.
In a year when tragedy became commonplace, the siege now grinding into its third week at the Japanese ambassador's residence added insult to injury.
The year began with the worst air crash in Peru's history when a Boeing 737 slammed into a mountain, killing all 123 passengers on board.
Six months after the first crash, Peru mourned 70 people who plunged to their death in the icy Pacific aboard a Boeing 727.
Peruvians reacted angrily to each accident -- especially when government investigations pointed to lax application of safety regulations.

The first plane crashed after losing height because it was allowed to carry too much cargo and the second due to adhesive tape covering sensors that left pilot Eric Schreiber without height or speed readings.
His final recorded words, transmitted later to the nation, still hang over Peru: "Where am I? Over land or sea?"
Guillermo Arbe, head of Lima research at Morgan Grenfell, said the plague of accidents was in part the consequence of poor safety standards.
"In Latin America in general there is less of a concern for preserving life than elsewhere," Arbe said.
In Peru, however, the authorities often had neither the will nor the resources to enforce the correct standards despite having the right legislation in place, he added.
The most glaring abuse of safety regulations was in the Andean highlands, where sleep-deprived drivers often steered -- or failed to steer -- overcrowded, ancient buses along the snaking roads.
Fatal plunges down mountainsides with 50-odd passengers have become such a regular event that the accidents receive little play in Lima's newspapers.
"There is so much negligence you have to believe the government does not care," said waiter Francisco Clavo. "Safety is a big problem. Disasters have become a way of life for us."
Natural disaster also struck Peru. In November, a powerful earthquake hit the south of the country, killing 16 people, leaving tens of thousands homeless and trapping dozens of miners underground.
Peru lies on a geological fault and is subject to frequent tremors.

Most people in the provinces live in adobe houses likely to cave in during a quake and, adding to the danger, thousands of free-lance, unlicensed miners work in temporary underground tunnels carved haphazardly into hillsides.
Safety apart, Peru also seemed especially unlucky in 1996.
Squeezed in between the two plane crashes came the most macabre accident of the year.

The town of Arequipa celebrated its anniversary with a grand party in August no different from that of any other year until fireworks struck an overhanging 10,000-volt electricity cable, causing it to fall and slash through about 1,500 people on a bridge.
Thirty-five people died from electrocution, 50 more were seriously injured and those under the bridge carried on celebrating, asssuming the noise came from exuberant partying.
"It was an incredibly dramatic year," Clavo said. "One disaster after the other. You just kept thinking the bad luck had to stop. But it didn't."

Even before the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels stormed the Japanese ambassador's residence Dec. 17, 1996 was the year in which Peruvians had to dismiss triumphalist talk that the country's 16 years of guerrilla conflict were over.

After several quiet years, Peru's much-larger, bloodier Shining Path rebel movement burst back onto its violent path in a spate of deadly attacks in July and August, raising public fears of a real comeback.
But, in the face of everything, a feeling pervades the country that 1997 cannot be worse than last year. Arbe also believed the resilient Peruvians would put the catastrophic year behind them.
"Memories are short and for many Peruvians daily life is a disaster anyway," he said.
